q: All metals have a tendency to lose electrons and form metal ions.
e: Metals are good reducing agents and easily oxidised by losing electrons to form positive metal ions.

q: All metals are good oxidizing agents and easily reduced by themselves.
e: All metals are good reducing agents and easily oxidised by themselves, not oxidizing agents.

q: The reactivity series of metals is a series in which metals are arranged in order of reactivity from lowest to highest.
e: The reactivity series arranges metals in order of reactivity from highest to lowest.

q: Metals above carbon can only be extracted from their ores by electrolysis.
e: Highly reactive metals above carbon in the reactivity series require electrolysis for extraction.

q: Metals below hydrogen can react vigorously with water and acids.
e: Metals below hydrogen can neither be reacted with water nor acid, and cannot easily be tarnished or corroded.

q: Potassium and sodium are very reactive and never found as free elements.
e: Due to their high reactivity, potassium and sodium are always found in combined states, not as free elements.

q: Potassium burns vigorously with a bright yellow flame.
e: Potassium burns vigorously with a bright lilac flame; sodium burns with a bright yellow flame.

q: Calcium burns quickly with a bright orange-red flame.
e: Calcium reacts with oxygen to burn quickly, producing a characteristic bright orange-red flame.

q: Magnesium burns quickly with a bright white flame.
e: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to burn quickly, producing a bright white flame.

q: Aluminium burns quickly with a bright yellow flame.
e: Aluminium reacts with oxygen to burn quickly, producing a bright yellow flame.

q: Zinc burns quickly with a light blue flame.
e: Zinc reacts with oxygen to burn quickly, producing a light blue flame.

q: Iron burns quickly with yellow sparks.
e: Iron reacts with oxygen to burn quickly, producing characteristic yellow sparks.

q: Tin, lead, copper, and mercury react slowly with oxygen even at high temperature.
e: These moderately reactive metals form a passive layer of oxide and react slowly even when heated.

q: Silver, gold, and platinum do not react with the oxygen in the air at all.
e: These noble metals are very unreactive and do not react with atmospheric oxygen.

q: Reactive metals such as potassium, sodium, and calcium react with cold water to produce the metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas.
e: Highly reactive metals displace hydrogen from cold water, forming metal hydroxides and hydrogen gas.

q: Potassium and sodium react violently with cold water, float, and catch fire.
e: The reaction is highly exothermic, producing enough heat to ignite the hydrogen gas formed.

q: Calcium reacts violently with cold water, floats, and catches fire.
e: Calcium reacts less vigorously with cold water compared to potassium and sodium.

q: Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water, but vigorously with steam.
e: Magnesium requires the higher energy of steam to react vigorously, forming magnesium oxide and hydrogen.

q: Aluminium apparently does not react with steam.
e: Aluminium forms a protective oxide layer that prevents further reaction with steam under normal conditions.

q: Zinc and iron react quite slowly with steam.
e: Zinc and iron are moderately reactive and react slowly with steam to form metal oxides and hydrogen gas.

q: Tin reacts with steam while heating.
e: Tin requires heating to react with steam, forming tin(IV) oxide and hydrogen gas.

q: Lead, copper, mercury, silver, gold, and platinum do not react with both water and steam.
e: These metals are below hydrogen in the reactivity series and do not react with water or steam.

q: The reactions of metals with dilute acids produce the corresponding metallic salts and oxygen gas.
e: The reactions of metals with dilute acids produce the corresponding metallic salts and hydrogen gas.

q: Potassium and sodium explode when added to dilute hydrochloric acid.
e: Due to their extreme reactivity, potassium and sodium react explosively with dilute acids.

q: Calcium reacts very fast with dilute hydrochloric acid.
e: Calcium is highly reactive and reacts very rapidly with dilute hydrochloric acid.

q: Magnesium reacts fast with dilute hydrochloric acid.
e: Magnesium is reactive and reacts fast with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce hydrogen gas.

q: Aluminium reacts moderately with dilute hydrochloric acid.
e: Aluminium reacts moderately with dilute hydrochloric acid after its protective oxide layer is penetrated.

q: Zinc, iron, and tin react slowly with dilute hydrochloric acid.
e: These moderately reactive metals react slowly with dilute hydrochloric acid.

q: Lead reacts very slowly with dilute hydrochloric acid.
e: Lead reacts very slowly, and the reaction often stops due to the formation of an insoluble lead(II) chloride layer.

q: Copper, mercury, silver, gold, and platinum have no reaction with dilute hydrochloric acid.
e: These metals are below hydrogen in the reactivity series and cannot displace hydrogen from dilute acids.

q: Displacement reaction is a chemical reaction in which a less reactive metal displaces a more reactive metal from its compound.
e: A displacement reaction is one in which a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound.

q: When a piece of magnesium is placed in a copper(II) sulphate solution, a brown solid forms on the surface of magnesium.
e: Magnesium is more reactive than copper and displaces it, forming solid brown copper metal.

q: In the displacement reaction between a metal and metal oxide, the less reactive metal will take the oxygen atom from the more reactive metal oxide.
e: The more reactive metal will take the oxygen atom from the less reactive metal oxide.

q: Gold, silver, and platinum are examples of metals that occur in the free state.
e: These noble metals are unreactive and are found in nature as free elements.

q: The oxide of iron and the sulphide of lead are examples of metals that occur in the free state.
e: The oxide of iron and the sulphide of lead are examples of metals found in the combined state.

q: Minerals are inorganic substances found in the Earth's crust.
e: Minerals are naturally occurring inorganic substances present in the Earth's crust.

q: Ores are those minerals from which metals are extracted economically.
e: An ore is a mineral that contains a high enough percentage of metal to make extraction economically viable.

q: Gangue refers to the desired metal compound in an ore.
e: Gangue refers to the earthly impurities and unwanted substances associated with the ore.

q: The process of extracting a metal from its ore is called metallurgy.
e: Metallurgy encompasses all processes involved in extracting pure metals from their ores.

q: The three major steps of extracting metal from its ore are concentration, isolation, and purification.
e: Metallurgy involves concentrating the ore, isolating the metal via reduction, and purifying the metal.

q: Removal of unwanted materials from the ore is known as concentration or dressing.
e: Concentration or dressing is the process of removing gangue like clay, sand, and stone from the ore.

q: Gravity separation is based on the difference in the magnetic properties of the ore components.
e: Gravity separation is based on the difference in the specific gravity of metal ores and mineral impurities.

q: Froth flotation process is generally used to concentrate the sulphide ores.
e: Sulphide ores get wet easily with oil, making froth flotation the ideal concentration method for them.

q: In the froth flotation process, the mineral particles become wet by water while the gangue particles become wet by oil.
e: In froth flotation, the mineral particles become wet by oil while the gangue particles become wet by water.

q: Pine oil is an appropriate oil used in the froth flotation process.
e: Pine oil is commonly used as the frothing agent in the froth flotation process.

q: Magnetic separation is used if either of the ores or the gangue has the magnetic property.
e: Magnetic separation relies on the difference in magnetic properties between the ore and the gangue.

q: In the chemical process, the mineral impurities of the ores are dissolved in a particular solution.
e: In the chemical process, the desired minerals of the ores are dissolved in a particular solution, not the impurities.

q: The concentrated ore is usually converted to an oxide before reduction because oxides are easier to reduce.
e: Metal oxides are more stable and easier to reduce to free metals compared to sulphides or carbonates.

q: Calcination involves heating the concentrated ores in a regular supply of air.
e: Calcination involves heating the concentrated ores in the absence of air.

q: During calcination, hydrated metal oxides and metal carbonates are converted to metal oxides.
e: Calcination removes volatile matter, moisture, and carbon dioxide, leaving behind the metal oxide.

q: Roasting is generally applied for sulphide ores.
e: Roasting heats sulphide ores in a regular supply of air to convert them into metal oxides and remove sulphur as sulphur dioxide.

q: During roasting, the ore is heated at a temperature above the melting point of the metal.
e: During roasting, the ore is heated at a temperature below the melting point of the metal.

q: Reduction of the metal oxide usually involves heating it with a reducing agent such as carbon, carbon monoxide, or another metal.
e: These reducing agents combine with the oxygen of the metal oxide to produce the free metal.

q: Metal extraction is an oxidation process.
e: Metal extraction is a reduction process because the metal ion gains electrons to become a free metal.

q: Flux is added to the ores to remove mineral impurities by forming metal slag.
e: Flux reacts with gangue at high temperatures to form a fusible product called slag.

q: Metal slag dissolves easily in molten metal.
e: Metal slag does not dissolve in molten metal; it floats on top due to its relatively light mass and is easily removed.

q: Smelting is the process where flux joins with impurities to form metal slag which is easily removed due to its relatively light mass.
e: Smelting involves the reduction of metallic oxides to free metals and the simultaneous removal of impurities as slag.

q: Purification by electrolysis is done to make the metal less pure than that obtained in the smelting process.
e: Purification by electrolysis is done to make the metal more pure than that obtained in the smelting process.

q: In Myanmar, copper and lead are rich mineral resources, and iron is a fairly rich resource.
e: Myanmar has abundant deposits of copper and lead, along with fairly rich iron ore resources.

q: Iron ore deposits in Myanmar are commonly found in Southern Shan State and Kayin State.
e: Iron ore deposits in Myanmar are commonly found in Northern Shan State and in Kachin State.

q: Copper deposits in Myanmar start from the lower Chindwin area through Sabe Taung, Kyesin Taung, Letpadaung Taung, Monywa, and Kawlin area.
e: These locations represent the major copper deposit regions extending through the northern part of Myanmar.

q: If a metal is less reactive than carbon, it can be extracted from its oxide by heating with carbon as a reducing agent.
e: Carbon can reduce the oxides of metals that are below it in the reactivity series.

q: Aluminium ore is bauxite, which is treated with sodium hydroxide to obtain pure alumina.
e: Bauxite is processed with sodium hydroxide to remove impurities and yield pure aluminium oxide (alumina).

q: Molten cryolite is added to dissolve alumina because it has a higher melting point than alumina.
e: Molten cryolite is added because it has a lower melting point than alumina, which reduces the temperature of fusion.

q: In the extraction of aluminium, aluminium is produced at the anode and oxygen is liberated at the cathode.
e: In the extraction of aluminium, aluminium is produced at the cathode and oxygen is liberated at the anode.

q: Aluminium is a silvery-white metal that is very ductile and malleable.
e: These are the characteristic physical properties of pure aluminium.

q: The melting point of aluminium is 660°C.
e: Aluminium has a relatively low melting point of 660°C compared to transition metals.

q: In moist air, a film of oxide is formed on the aluminium surface which prevents any further attack on the underlying metal.
e: This protective aluminium oxide layer is chemically inert and prevents corrosion.

q: Aluminium reacts rapidly with dilute sulphuric acid to give aluminium sulphate and oxygen gas.
e: Aluminium reacts slowly with dilute sulphuric acid to give aluminium sulphate and hydrogen gas.

q: When aluminium is exposed to hot concentrated sulphuric acid, the result is aluminium sulphate, water, and sulphur dioxide.
e: Hot concentrated sulphuric acid acts as an oxidizing agent, producing sulphur dioxide gas.

q: Both dilute and concentrated nitric acids react very rapidly with aluminium.
e: Both dilute and concentrated nitric acids react very slowly with aluminium due to the protective oxide layer.

q: Aluminium reacts with alkalis, making it an amphoteric metal.
e: Aluminium is amphoteric because it can react with both acids and alkalis.

q: The reduction of a metallic oxide with aluminium is known as the Thermite reaction.
e: The Thermite reaction uses aluminium as a reducing agent to extract metals like iron from their oxides, releasing a lot of heat.

q: Haematite ($Fe_2O_3$) and magnetite ($Fe_3O_4$) ores are suitable for the extraction of iron.
e: These are the primary iron ores used in the blast furnace for iron extraction.

q: In the blast furnace, coke burns to produce carbon monoxide directly from oxygen.
e: In the blast furnace, coke burns to produce carbon dioxide, which then reacts with more carbon to form carbon monoxide.

q: Carbon monoxide reduces the oxides of iron to iron in the blast furnace.
e: Carbon monoxide is the primary reducing agent that converts iron oxides to molten iron.

q: Limestone breaks down due to the heat of the furnace to form calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.
e: Calcium carbonate decomposes thermally to form calcium oxide, which acts as a basic flux.

q: Calcium oxide reacts with sand (silicon dioxide) to form calcium silicate, which is known as slag.
e: Calcium silicate ($CaSiO_3$) is the slag that floats on molten iron and is removed.

q: The iron obtained from the blast furnace is known as pig or cast iron and contains about 4% carbon.
e: Pig iron is the crude iron product from the blast furnace, containing approximately 4% carbon and other impurities.

q: Wrought iron is the impurest form of industrial iron.
e: Wrought iron is the purest form of industrial iron, obtained by removing impurities from pig iron.

q: Pure iron is soft, malleable, and rusts easily in damp air.
e: Unlike its alloys, pure iron is relatively soft and highly susceptible to rusting.

q: Unlike most other metals, pure iron is magnetic.
e: Iron is one of the few elements that exhibit strong ferromagnetism at room temperature.

q: The melting point of pure iron is 1538°C.
e: Pure iron has a high melting point of 1538°C.

q: When chlorine passes over heated iron, iron is oxidised to iron(II) chloride.
e: When chlorine passes over heated iron, iron is oxidised to iron(III) chloride.

q: When a mixture of iron filings and sulphur powder is heated, black iron(II) sulphide is formed.
e: Iron reacts with sulphur upon heating to form black iron(II) sulphide ($FeS$).

q: Iron reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to form iron(III) sulphate and hydrogen gas.
e: Iron reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to form iron(II) sulphate and hydrogen gas.

q: With hot concentrated sulphuric acid, iron gives iron(III) sulphate, water, and sulphur dioxide.
e: Hot concentrated sulphuric acid oxidizes iron to the +3 oxidation state, producing sulphur dioxide.

q: Iron reacts with hydrochloric acid to form iron(II) chloride and hydrogen gas because the production of hydrogen gas prevents further oxidation of $Fe^{2+}$ to $Fe^{3+}$.
e: The hydrogen gas produced acts as a reducing environment, keeping iron in the +2 oxidation state.

q: The lead ore, galena ($PbS$), is ground into small particles and put through a flotation process.
e: Galena is concentrated using the froth flotation process before extraction.

q: In the extraction of lead, the powder is heated to more than 1370°C, producing lead(II) oxide and volatile sulphur dioxide.
e: This roasting step converts lead(II) sulphide to lead(II) oxide.

q: The resulting lead(II) oxide is further heated in a blast furnace with oxygen to produce molten lead.
e: The resulting lead(II) oxide is further heated in a blast furnace with carbon to produce molten lead.

q: At the refining stage, lead is about 95% pure and is further refined to get greater than 99% purity.
e: Initial reduction yields ~95% pure lead, which is then refined by melting and skimming to exceed 99% purity.

q: Lead is a bluish-grey metal and is the softest of the metals in common use.
e: Lead is very soft and can be easily pressed into any form.

q: Lead is a good conductor of electricity and heat.
e: Lead is a poor conductor of electricity and heat compared to other common metals.

q: On exposure to air, lead is tarnished owing to the formation of a layer of hydroxide and carbonate.
e: This protective layer prevents further attack on the underlying lead metal.

q: The melting point of lead is 328°C.
e: Lead has a relatively low melting point of 328°C.

q: Lead does not react with water or steam.
e: Lead is below hydrogen in the reactivity series and does not react with water or steam.

q: Dilute sulphuric acid has a vigorous action upon lead to form lead(II) sulphate and hydrogen gas.
e: Dilute sulphuric acid has no appreciable action upon lead due to the formation of an insoluble lead(II) sulphate layer.

q: Hot concentrated sulphuric acid reacts with lead to form lead(II) sulphate, water, and sulphur dioxide.
e: Hot concentrated sulphuric acid acts as an oxidizing agent, reacting with lead to produce sulphur dioxide.

q: Lead reacts with dilute nitric acid to form lead(II) nitrate, water, and nitrogen oxide.
e: Dilute nitric acid oxidizes lead, producing nitrogen oxide ($NO$) gas.

q: Lead reacts with hot concentrated nitric acid to form lead(II) nitrate, water, and nitrogen dioxide.
e: Concentrated nitric acid is a stronger oxidizing agent, producing nitrogen dioxide ($NO_2$) gas.

q: The main source of copper ore is copper pyrites, also known as chalcopyrite ($CuFeS_2$).
e: Chalcopyrite is the most abundant and economically important copper ore.

q: Copper ore typically contains a high percentage of copper and does not need to be concentrated.
e: Copper ore typically contains a low percentage of copper and has to be concentrated before refining.

q: In the extraction of copper, the concentrated ore is heated strongly with silicon dioxide and air or oxygen in a furnace.
e: This smelting process converts the ore into copper(I) sulphide and removes iron as slag.

q: The copper in copper pyrites is reduced to copper(II) sulphide.
e: The copper in copper pyrites is reduced to copper(I) sulphide ($Cu_2S$).

q: The iron in copper pyrites is converted into an iron(II) silicate slag which is removed.
e: Iron reacts with silicon dioxide to form iron(II) silicate slag ($FeSiO_3$), which is separated.

q: Most of the sulphur in copper pyrites turns into sulphur trioxide gas.
e: Most of the sulphur in copper pyrites turns into sulphur dioxide ($SO_2$) gas.

q: The copper(I) sulphide produced is converted to copper with a final blast of air.
e: Air oxidizes the sulphur in copper(I) sulphide to sulphur dioxide, leaving behind blister copper.

q: The end product, blister copper, is a porous brittle form of copper which is about 98~99.5% pure.
e: Blister copper gets its name from the blisters formed by escaping sulphur dioxide gas.

q: Copper is refined by electrolysis to get at least 99.92% purity.
e: Electrolytic refining is the final step to achieve high-purity copper suitable for electrical applications.

q: Copper is a reddish coloured metal, and a freshly exposed surface has a pinkish-orange colour.
e: This distinctive colour is a key physical property of pure copper.

q: The melting point of copper is 1084°C.
e: Copper has a melting point of 1084°C.

q: Copper can react with non-oxidising acids such as dilute hydrochloric acid.
e: Copper can react with oxidising acids such as concentrated sulphuric acid and both dilute and concentrated nitric acids.

q: The most common reaction product of heated copper and oxygen is copper(I) oxide.
e: The most common reaction product of heated copper and oxygen is copper(II) oxide ($CuO$).

q: In a pure metal, atoms are packed regularly in layers that can slide over one another when force is applied.
e: This regular packing and sliding ability is why pure metals are generally soft and malleable.

q: Pure metals are widely used because they are very hard and do not react with air and water.
e: Pure metals are not widely used because many are soft and may react with air and water, resulting in corrosion.

q: When a pure metal is alloyed, atoms of the added element have the same sizes as those of the pure metal.
e: When a pure metal is alloyed, atoms of the added element have different sizes from those of the pure metal.

q: The atoms of different sizes in an alloy cannot slide over each other easily, making the alloy harder than pure metals.
e: The disruption of the regular atomic layers by different-sized atoms increases the hardness and strength of the alloy.

q: Mixing molten tin and copper gives a gold-coloured alloy called brass.
e: Mixing molten tin and copper gives a gold-coloured alloy called bronze.

q: Bronze has much greater strength, hardness, and corrosion resistance than pure copper and tin.
e: Alloying improves the mechanical properties and durability of the base metals.

q: Steel is an alloy of iron containing carbon and other metals.
e: Steel is primarily an alloy of iron and carbon, often with other metals added to modify its properties.

q: Cupronickel contains 75% copper and 25% nickel, and is used for coins.
e: Cupronickel is hard, shining, and lasting, making it ideal for coinage.

q: Brass contains 70% copper and 30% zinc, and is used for ship boilers.
e: Brass does not corrode easily, which is why it is used in ship boilers and other marine applications.

q: Bronze contains 90% copper and 10% tin, and is used for ship propellers.
e: Bronze is very hard and strong, making it suitable for ship propellers.

q: Solder contains 70% lead and 30% tin, and has a high melting point.
e: Solder contains 70% lead and 30% tin, and has a low melting point, making it useful for soldering wires.

q: Duralumin contains 93% aluminium, 3% copper, 3% magnesium, and 1% manganese, and is light and strong.
e: Duralumin's light weight and high strength make it ideal for aeroplane bodies and bullet trains.

q: Magnalium contains 70% aluminium and 30% magnesium, and is hard but light.
e: Magnalium is used in aircraft structures due to its favorable strength-to-weight ratio.

q: Pink gold contains 75% gold, 20% copper, and 5% silver.
e: This specific composition gives pink gold its soft, malleable, and ductile properties for jewellery.

q: Mild steel contains 99.7% iron and 0.3% carbon, and is hard and strong.
e: Mild steel is widely used for car bodies, buildings, ships, and machinery.

q: Hard steel contains 99% iron and 1% carbon, and is hard and brittle.
e: The higher carbon content makes hard steel suitable for cutting tools, razor blades, and chisels.

q: Soft steel contains 99.8% iron and 0.2% carbon, and is malleable and ductile.
e: Soft steel is used for cables, nails, and chains due to its malleability and ductility.

q: Stainless steel contains 73% iron, 18% chromium, 8% nickel, and 1% carbon, and is hard and rustproof.
e: Chromium and nickel provide stainless steel with excellent corrosion resistance, making it ideal for cutlery and surgical instruments.

q: Nickel steel contains 98~96% iron, 2~4% nickel, and trace carbon, and is hard, elastic, and rustproof.
e: Nickel steel is used for cables, automobile, and aeroplane parts.

q: Tungsten steel contains 83~72% iron, 14~20% tungsten, 3~8% chromium, and trace carbon, and is hard with resistance to corrosion.
e: Tungsten steel is used for high-speed cutting tools and springs.

q: Manganese steel contains 89~88% iron, 11~12% manganese, and trace carbon, and is extremely hard with a high melting point.
e: Manganese steel is used for rail tracks and rock crushers due to its extreme hardness.

q: Corrosion is the deterioration of metals as a result of chemical reaction depending on the type of metal and environmental conditions.
e: Corrosion leads to a loss of structural integrity and attractiveness in metals.

q: Corrosion of iron is called tarnishing.
e: Corrosion of iron is specifically called rusting.

q: Most metals, except gold, can be corroded because they oxidise.
e: Gold is highly unreactive and does not oxidise under normal environmental conditions.

q: Silver reacts with sulphur in the air to form silver sulphide ($Ag_2S$) and turns black.
e: This black tarnish is a common example of silver corrosion.

q: Copper reacts with moist carbon dioxide in the air and gets a green coat called verdigris ($CuCO_3 \cdot Cu(OH)_2$).
e: Verdigris is the characteristic green patina that forms on corroded copper.

q: Iron acquires a coating of a brown flaky substance called rust ($Fe_2O_3 \cdot xH_2O$).
e: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, which flakes off and exposes fresh iron to further corrosion.

q: Only air is necessary for the rusting of iron.
e: Both air (oxygen) and moisture (water) are necessary for the rusting of iron.

q: Chrome plating is a method of applying a thin layer of chromium onto a metal object to provide corrosion resistance.
e: Chromium plating is both decorative and protective against corrosion.

q: Tin plating is commonly used in making food cans.
e: Tin is non-toxic and resistant to corrosion, making it safe for food storage.

q: Galvanising is the process of immersing iron or steel in molten zinc to produce a corrosion-resistant layer.
e: Galvanising protects iron exposed to non-corrosive mediums like air.

q: Sacrificial protection is used to protect iron exposed to a non-corrosive medium.
e: Sacrificial protection is used to protect iron exposed to a corrosive medium, such as seawater.

q: In sacrificial protection, a zinc bar is attached to iron or steel.
e: Zinc is more reactive than iron and will oxidise (sacrifice itself) to protect the iron.

q: Making alloys can improve the properties of metals in terms of strength, durability, conductivity, and corrosion resistance.
e: Alloying is a primary method for enhancing the overall performance of base metals.

q: Metal recycling can be beneficial to the environment by increasing mining operations.
e: Metal recycling is beneficial because it reduces mining operations, air and water pollution, and conserves fossil fuel reserves.

q: The main stages of metal recycling are collection, sorting, processing, and distribution.
e: These four stages ensure that scrap metal is efficiently converted back into usable material.

q: In the processing stage of aluminium recycling, purification is a mechanical operation.
e: In the processing stage, purification is a chemical operation, mostly involving electrolysis.

q: Solidifying in the metal recycling process is a chemical operation to a specific shape.
e: Solidifying in the metal recycling process is a mechanical operation to form a specific shape.

q: Potash alum ($K_2SO_4 \cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3 \cdot 24H_2O$) can be used in water purification, leather tanning, and dyeing.
e: Potash alum is a useful aluminium compound with various industrial and chemical applications.

q: Lead(II,IV) oxide (Red lead, $Pb_3O_4$) can be used for surface coating.
e: Red lead is commonly used as a protective primer or surface coating to prevent rust.

q: Bordeaux mixture, a suspension of copper(II) sulphate and calcium hydroxide, is used to control fungus on grapes, melons, and other berries.
e: Bordeaux mixture is a well-known fungicide used in agriculture.
